quote: A cone-dense area centralis is present dorsotemporal to the optic nerve, similar to other carnivores.
note: Dorsotemporal retina looks forward and slightly down.

taxon: Primates, squirrels, red kangaroo, pig; marsupials; carnivores, rodents, Cetacea; ungulates
value: absent in primates, squirrels, red kangaroo and pig; retinal tapetum in marsupials and the fruit bat; choroidal cellulosum in carnivores, rodents and Cetacea; fibrosum in cow, sheep, goat and horse

source.authors: Ollivier FJ, Samuelson DA, Brooks DE, Lewis PA, Kallberg ME, Komáromy AM
source.title: Comparative morphology of the tapetum lucidum (among selected species)

quote: Some species (primates, squirrels, birds, red kangaroo and pig) do not have this structure and they usually are diurnal animals.
note: Authors now known (the earlier sheet could not find them): Ollivier, Samuelson, Brooks, Lewis, Kallberg, Komáromy. Young et al. 1988 report a tapetum fibrosum in Kogia and Tursiops, which conflicts with 'cellulosum' for Cetacea here.

source.authors: Glösmann M, Steiner M, Peichl L, Ahnelt PK
source.title: Cone photoreceptors and potential UV vision in a subterranean insectivore, the European mole

quote: Similar to most mammals, two cone opsins, shortwave-sensitive (S) and middle-to-long-wave-sensitive (M), are present.
note: Retina 0.75 mm2, about 100,000 photoreceptors, 10 to 12% cones; S opsin sequence points to UV sensitivity; lens transmits to 300 nm. European mole holds 17,116 of 28,258 mole records (61%).

method: inferred from lens transmission and opsin tuning sites

source.authors: Glösmann M, Steiner M, Peichl L, Ahnelt PK
source.title: Cone photoreceptors and potential UV vision in a subterranean insectivore, the European mole

quote: Partial sequencing of the S opsin gene strongly supports UV sensitivity of the mole S cone photopigment.
note: Lower bound from 'The lens transmits light down to 300 nm'; upper bound 600 is my guess from an M cone and is unmeasured. Authors conclude photopic vision and UV sensitivity play a role.

source.authors: Pettigrew JD, Bhagwandin A, Haagensen M, Manger PR
source.title: Visual acuity and heterogeneities of retinal ganglion cell densities and the tapetum lucidum of the African elephant (Loxodonta africana)

quote: our calculations indicate that the elephant has a maximal visual acuity of between 13.16 and 14.37 cycles/degree.
note: Three high-density regions: upper temporal area, horizontal streak, nasal area. Far above the one behavioural measure (48 arcmin, about 0.6 cpd).

value: heterogeneous tapetum, strongest behind the temporal and nasal ganglion cell densities

source.authors: Pettigrew JD, Bhagwandin A, Haagensen M, Manger PR
source.title: Visual acuity and heterogeneities of retinal ganglion cell densities and the tapetum lucidum of the African elephant (Loxodonta africana)

quote: We observed a heterogeneous structure of a tapetum lucidum, the cells of which were found to be most strongly aggregated behind the temporal and nasal densities of retinal ganglion cells.

source.authors: Yokoyama S, Takenaka N, Agnew D, Shoshani J
source.title: Elephants and human color-blind deuteranopes have identical sets of visual pigments

quote: elephants (Loxodonta africana and Elephas maximus) use RH1, SWS1, and LWS pigments, which are maximally sensitive to 496, 419, and 552 nm, respectively.
note: Fills the earlier sheet's unfinished elephant colour row. The authors compare them with human deuteranopes. Two values in one line because the source gives them together.

source.authors: Shyan-Norwalt MR, Peterson J, Milankow B, Staggs TE, Dale R
source.title: Initial findings on visual acuity thresholds in an African elephant (Loxodonta africana)

quote: one African elephant cow demonstrated a visual acuity of 48' of arc. This represents the ability to discriminate a gap as small as 2.75 cm in a stimulus 196 cm from the eye.
note: Converted as 30 / 48 arcmin = 0.63 (gap taken as half a cycle). Asian elephants 8 to 11 arcmin near the trunk tip (earlier studies, same abstract). Year 2009 in the collection (issue year given as 2010 in the earlier sheet).

method: anatomical: ganglion cell density, one retina

source.authors: Pettigrew JD, Manger PR
source.title: Retinal ganglion cell density of the black rhinoceros (Diceros bicornis): calculating visual resolution

quote: Our calculations indicate that the rhinoceros has a visual resolution of 6 cycles/degree.
note: Long thin horizontal streak with temporal and nasal specializations; density biased to the upper retina, so it looks mostly below the horizon. Fills the earlier sheet's refused page.

source.authors: Arrese CA, Archer M, Runham PB, Dunlop SA, Beazley LD
source.title: Visual system in a diurnal marsupial, the numbat (Myrmecobius fasciatus): retinal organization, visual acuity and visual fields

quote: was found to be 6.3 cycles per degree. The value was similar to that of 5.2 cycles per degree estimated by behavioral tests.
note: Binocular overlap 80 degrees, total field about 240 degrees; a wide static pupil.

source.authors: Arrese CA, Archer M, Beazley LD
source.title: Visual capabilities in a crepuscular marsupial, the honey possum (Tarsipes rostratus): a visual approach to ecology

quote: The remarkable total field of view, approaching 240° of visual angle and including a binocular overlap of 80° in the horizontal plane, provides an efficient predator detection capacity.
note: Acuity 0.63 cycles/degree in daylight, 0.60 in moonlight and starlight (same abstract).

source.authors: Ebeling W, Natoli RC, Hemmi JM

note: Quokka, quenda, honey possum and fat-tailed dunnart earlier described as trichromatic. DOI from the collection index (the earlier sheet had none). Full text on disk (CC BY).

source.authors: Hemmi JM, Mark RF

source.authors: Emerling CA, Springer MS

source.journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
